title: New Scientist Story Ideas — Psychotherapy — September 2026

studies.title: Exposure therapy for spider phobia works less well when progesterone is high
studies.ns_score_reason: genuinely new question ("when does therapy work?") with a clean biological hook, held back by a small sample and a null result on the headline comparison
studies.ns_check: Not verified — SerpAPI unavailable this run
studies.the_study: Researchers recruited 45 women with spider phobia, grouped by hormonal status — early-to-mid follicular phase, mid-luteal phase, or using hormonal contraceptives — and put them through group exposure therapy, measuring fear and avoidance at baseline, one week after, and 12–14 weeks later. Everyone improved. Menstrual cycle group made no difference, but women with higher progesterone on the actual day of the exposure session showed less improvement in behavioral avoidance, the measure that tracks what people will physically do rather than what they say they feel.
studies.why_it_matters: It raises the possibility that the *timing* of a therapy session against a person's internal hormonal rhythm shapes how much fear extinction sticks — a variable no clinic currently considers. This is preliminary and needs replication in far larger samples before anyone reschedules an appointment.
studies.pitch_angle: Everything we know about psychotherapy is about *who* it works for and *why*; almost nothing about *when*. Open on a woman standing in front of a tarantula tank on a Tuesday, and the question of whether next Tuesday would have gone better. Lead with the progesterone-avoidance link and the concept of "bio-rhythm informed psychotherapy". Call Susanne Fischer and Ulrike Ehlert at the University of Zurich, and get an independent fear-extinction researcher to say how much weight 45 participants can carry.
studies.wider_angle: A feature on the neglect of hormonal variation across clinical trial design generally — from analgesia to vaccines to psychotherapy — and the growing push to treat the menstrual cycle as a measured variable rather than noise. Fits a health-policy or women's-health-focused outlet, or a long read for a general-interest magazine.
studies.caveats: Small N (45), three-arm design with unequal hormonal groups, no randomization to cycle phase (participants were enrolled according to their own cycles), single site, the primary group comparison was null and the hormone finding is a secondary correlational result, self-reported measures alongside the behavioral test.

studies.title: People want their psilocybin natural, even when the synthetic version is chemically identical
studies.ns_score_reason: a clean, quotable irrationality in how people think about psychedelic medicine, with decent sample sizes; limited by the fact that intentions are not behavior
studies.ns_check: Not verified — SerpAPI unavailable this run
studies.the_study: Across two studies with 1,102 participants in total, researchers measured how willing people were to use psilocybin for a mental health problem compared with psychotherapy or conventional psychiatric medication. Psilocybin came last. And in the second study, people were significantly more willing to take psilocybin "isolated from mushrooms" than an identical synthetic version, or a synthetic analog producing the same biological effects. Willingness was higher in men, in younger people, and in those reporting more current depression, more mindfulness — and more narcissism.
studies.why_it_matters: If regulators approve psilocybin, uptake will be shaped by a naturalness bias that has no pharmacological basis, and by the fact that the public still ranks it below talking therapy. That is a marketing and public-health problem before it is a clinical one.
studies.pitch_angle: Hype notwithstanding, the public is less keen on psychedelic therapy than on ordinary talking therapy — and prefers its molecules to have come out of a mushroom. Open on the identical-molecule comparison, which is a textbook naturalness fallacy running straight into a soon-to-be-regulated medicine. Call Brian Meier at Gettysburg College, and Matthew Johnson (Medical College of Georgia) for the clinical-translation view.
studies.wider_angle: A consumer-psychology piece on the "appeal to nature" across medicine and food — supplements, bioidentical hormones, natural flavorings — and how the psychedelics industry is already positioning itself around botanical extracts. Fits a business or consumer-affairs outlet.
studies.caveats: Hypothetical intentions rather than real uptake; online convenience samples of unclear representativeness; self-reported depression and personality measures; population may not generalize beyond the US.

studies.title: Psychotherapy use in the US jumped 41 per cent in four years — and worsening mental health explains only a third of it
studies.ns_score_reason: very large, well-analyzed national dataset with a genuinely unexplained residual, but it is a trends paper without a single striking mechanism
studies.the_study: Using 147,488 respondents from the 2019–2023 National Health Interview Surveys, researchers tracked mental health care use before and after the pandemic. Any mental health care rose from 19.2 per cent to 23.8 per cent; psychotherapy use rose from 9.5 per cent to 13.4 per cent, a 41 per cent increase. Decomposition analysis attributed 36.7 per cent of the overall rise to changes in anxiety and depression symptoms and 11.3 per cent to insurance coverage — leaving roughly half unaccounted for.
studies.why_it_matters: The standard story is that more Americans are in therapy because more Americans are unwell. This says symptoms and insurance together explain under half the surge, pointing to shifts in help-seeking, stigma, telehealth and expectation that nobody has yet quantified.
studies.pitch_angle: Therapy went mainstream faster than distress did. Open on the missing half of the increase and what plausibly fills it — teletherapy apps, a post-2020 collapse in stigma, therapy as self-improvement rather than treatment. Call Y. Nina Gao and Mark Olfson at Columbia; ask them directly what they think the unexplained share is.
studies.wider_angle: A trend piece on therapy as a consumer category — waitlists, subscription platforms, the workforce shortage it creates — and whether a system built for illness can absorb a population seeking optimization. Fits a business, health-policy or general-interest outlet.
studies.caveats: Observational survey data, cannot establish causation; self-reported service use and symptoms; decomposition results depend on model specification; US-only.

studies.title: Children's therapy works better when the therapist unconsciously mirrors them
studies.ns_score_reason: an appealing, very visual mechanism tested with real coded sessions and a mediation model; correlational within a trial, and the mediator is measured in-session
studies.ns_check: Not verified — SerpAPI unavailable this run
studies.the_study: Researchers coded 245 sessions from early, middle and late phases of Mentalization-Based Treatment for Children, involving 95 children (mean age 7.8) with internalizing and externalizing problems and 16 therapists. Therapists who showed more nonverbal coordination — matching posture, rhythm and movement during play — had children who regulated their emotions better within the session, and that in-session regulation predicted lower total problem scores and better parent-reported emotion regulation over treatment. The effect of nonverbal coordination on outcomes ran entirely through in-session regulation; the direct path was not significant.
studies.why_it_matters: It gives an empirical spine to something child therapists do intuitively, and suggests the active ingredient in play therapy may be bodily synchrony rather than anything said out loud.
studies.pitch_angle: The most important thing a child therapist does may happen below the neck. Open in a playroom where the therapist is silently matching a seven-year-old's tempo with a toy car. Hook: a measured, mediated pathway from therapist movement to parent-reported behavior at home. Call Sibel Halfon at Istanbul Bilgi University; pair with an interpersonal-synchrony researcher for scepticism about coding-based mediation.
studies.wider_angle: A broader feature on interpersonal synchrony — in parenting, teaching, music ensembles, therapy — and what happens when this research meets video calls, where bodily coordination largely breaks down. Fits a psychology-focused outlet or an education trade title.
studies.caveats: Secondary analysis within a clinical trial; mediation from observational session data cannot establish causation; small number of therapists (16) limits generalization; parent-reported outcomes; single center.

studies.title: Social life doesn't improve during therapy — it improves for years afterward
studies.ns_score_reason: a nice reversal of expectation with 2.5 years of follow-up in 370 patients; limited to self-report instruments and a naturalistic design
studies.ns_check: Not verified — SerpAPI unavailable this run
studies.the_study: Following 370 Norwegian adult outpatients through open-ended psychotherapy with up to 2.5 years of follow-up, researchers tracked the quantity and quality of social relationships alongside a measure of self-affiliation — how warmly people treat themselves. Social connection did not change from before to after treatment. It grew steadily *after* therapy ended, particularly in support and in non-family relationships. And the two measures fed each other in lagged sequence: better social connection predicted more self-kindness at the next assessment, which predicted better social connection after that.
studies.why_it_matters: Therapy outcomes are almost always measured at discharge, which may be exactly the wrong moment to look for relational change. It also offers evidence for the long-suspected loop between self-compassion and friendship running in both directions.
studies.pitch_angle: Therapy's social payoff arrives late — sometimes years after the last session. Open on a patient who left treatment feeling no more connected than when they arrived, and whose friendships slowly widened afterward. Lead on the reciprocal loop between being kind to yourself and having people around you. Call Erkki Heinonen (University of Oslo / Finnish Institute for Health and Welfare) or first author Anna Voldstad at Oxford.
studies.wider_angle: A feature on how mental health services measure success — discharge-day symptom scores versus the things patients actually want, such as friends, work and a life — and the case for long-tail outcome tracking. Fits a health-services or specialist psychiatry publication.
studies.caveats: Naturalistic observational design, no control group, cannot establish causation; entirely self-reported measures; attrition likely across 2.5 years; Norwegian outpatient sample may not generalize.

studies.title: AI writes usable therapy notes — but misses what clinicians notice
studies.ns_score_reason: first head-to-head, blinded comparison on a task AI is being sold into right now; the result is a measured "not yet", which is honest but less headline-grabbing
studies.the_study: Researchers generated 1,008 summaries — 504 written by clinicians and 504 by a large language model using a multi-step prompting pipeline — covering 108 five-minute segments from 36 real therapy sessions. Judges blinded to authorship rated factual consistency, preservation of salient meaning, and clinical value. Clinicians won overall, but the model was *better* at preserving central themes, and the two were indistinguishable on clinical value when describing the therapeutic relationship and the client's internal functioning.
studies.why_it_matters: Documentation is one of the biggest time sinks in mental health care, and this is the first direct evidence on where AI drafting is adequate and where it is not — supporting a draft-and-review workflow rather than replacement.
studies.pitch_angle: An AI can summarize your therapy session, and blinded judges rated it roughly as insightful as a human on the therapeutic relationship — the bit you would least expect a machine to get. Open on a therapist who spends an hour each evening on notes. Call Dana Atzil-Slonim at Bar-Ilan University; ask what clients think about a model reading their sessions.
studies.wider_angle: A privacy and consent story: therapy transcripts are among the most sensitive records that exist, and AI scribes are entering clinics faster than governance frameworks. Fits a technology-policy or investigative outlet.
studies.caveats: Only 36 sessions, judged at five-minute segment level rather than whole sessions; evaluation by expert raters, not by the clinicians or clients involved; no test of downstream effects on care; single research pipeline, results may not transfer to commercial tools.

studies.title: Automated sentiment analysis of therapy sessions barely matches what human coders see
studies.ns_score_reason: a useful negative result against a fast-growing assumption, though the subject matter is one step removed from readers' own lives
studies.ns_check: Not verified — SerpAPI unavailable this run
studies.the_study: Using 108 early therapy sessions, trained human coders rated positive, negative and neutral affect turn by turn. The researchers then ran the same transcripts through a dictionary method (LIWC) and a neural language model (XLM-T). At the level of individual conversational turns, the automated tools showed essentially no convergence with human ratings; agreement appeared only weakly when averaged across whole sessions. Automated negativity tracked human coding better for clients' speech than therapists'. Both tools nonetheless predicted therapist- and client-rated early alliance.
studies.why_it_matters: A lot of computational psychotherapy research, and a growing number of products, assume text sentiment is a proxy for emotion in the room. Turn by turn, it isn't — though it may still carry signal about the relationship.
studies.pitch_angle: Machines can tell you something about a therapeutic relationship while getting almost every individual moment wrong. Open on a single exchange where a client says something upbeat in a devastated tone. Lead with the near-zero turn-level convergence. Call Paul Peluso at Florida State University, and pair with someone building AI therapy-monitoring tools for a response.
studies.wider_angle: A skeptical feature on sentiment analysis across the board — customer service, social media mood tracking, political forecasting — and the systematic errors that follow from treating words as feelings. Fits a technology or data-science outlet.
studies.caveats: 108 sessions from one dataset; human coding is itself imperfect as a gold standard; two specific tools tested, results may not extend to newer models; alliance outcomes are self-reported.

studies.title: Whether a patient had a "sudden gain" in therapy depends on which questionnaire you used
studies.ns_score_reason: a solid, uncomfortable result for a whole literature, in a large sample; the topic requires some setup for general readers
studies.ns_check: Not verified — SerpAPI unavailable this run
studies.the_study: "Sudden gains" — abrupt, lasting drops in symptoms between sessions — are a well-studied phenomenon linked to better outcomes. Analyzing data from 937 university students in a five-week internet-delivered treatment for depression and anxiety, researchers looked for sudden gains using both standard scales (PHQ-9, GAD-7) and their ultra-brief two-item versions. The measures disagreed on both how many sudden gains occurred and, critically, *which individuals* had them.
studies.why_it_matters: If a phenomenon's presence in a given person changes depending on the instrument, findings across the sudden-gains literature may not be comparable — a measurement problem sitting underneath a body of research about how therapy actually works.
studies.pitch_angle: One of psychotherapy research's most appealing ideas — the week everything suddenly shifts — may be partly an artifact of the questionnaire. Open on the lived experience of a sudden gain, then pull the rug. Call Blake Dear at Macquarie University's eCentreClinic; ask a sudden-gains researcher elsewhere whether they accept the critique.
studies.wider_angle: A measurement-validity feature: how much of psychology's knowledge base is contingent on the specific scales in use, from depression to personality to wellbeing indices. Fits a research-culture or metascience-oriented outlet.
studies.caveats: Secondary analysis of existing trial data; university student sample in a brief internet-delivered treatment may not generalize to face-to-face clinical care; all outcomes self-reported.

studies.title: Trauma-focused therapy for PTSD plus addiction helps veterans more than civilians
studies.ns_score_reason: large pooled patient-level dataset and a real moderation finding, but the effect is confined to alcohol outcomes and the population is specialized
studies.ns_check: Not verified — SerpAPI unavailable this run
studies.the_study: Pooling individual patient data from 26 randomized trials (n=3,228) in the Project Harmony meta-analysis, researchers tested whether veteran status changes how well psychotherapy works for co-occurring PTSD and substance use disorder. Both trauma-focused therapy for PTSD alone and integrated therapy targeting both conditions beat treatment as usual on alcohol use severity — and the advantage was larger for veterans than for civilians. There was no such difference for PTSD symptoms or drug use.
studies.why_it_matters: It is the first patient-level test of a long-suspected divide, and it addresses the persistent clinical worry that trauma-focused therapy destabilizes people who are drinking. It did not; it helped.
studies.pitch_angle: Clinicians have long hesitated to take people with active addictions into trauma-focused therapy. This pooled analysis of 3,228 patients suggests the opposite of harm — and that veterans benefit more than civilians, for reasons nobody can yet explain. Call Shannon Blakey at RTI International or Denise Hien at Rutgers; press them on whether it is the veterans or the veteran-oriented services that differ.
studies.wider_angle: A piece on why so much PTSD evidence comes from military samples, and what that means for civilian survivors of assault, accidents and displacement who are treated on the strength of it. Fits a specialist psychiatry publication or a long-read current-affairs outlet.
studies.caveats: Secondary analysis of trial data with propensity-score weighting, not a randomized comparison of veterans versus civilians; effect limited to one outcome domain; several authors are authors of the COPE treatment manual and one reports extensive industry ties and patents; funded by the National Institute on Alcohol Abuse and Alcoholism.

studies.title: Muslim clients say they censor their faith in the therapy room
studies.journal: Psychology and Psychotherapy: Theory, Research and Practice
studies.ns_score_reason: a rich, well-conducted qualitative study on a real gap in service delivery; qualitative design caps how far it can be pushed as news
studies.ns_check: Not verified — SerpAPI unavailable this run
studies.the_study: Twenty-five Muslim adults in the UK who had received therapy in NHS and private settings were interviewed about how religion was handled. Reflexive thematic analysis identified two patterns: barriers — therapists' visible discomfort and limited knowledge, secular service frameworks, and clients' resulting self-censorship — and recommendations, including proactive rather than reactive engagement with faith and organizational change to legitimize religion as clinically relevant material.
studies.why_it_matters: For many clients, religion is not an add-on but the organizing frame of their distress and their coping. If they edit it out to make therapists comfortable, the therapy is working on an incomplete account.
studies.pitch_angle: Clients are managing their therapists' discomfort about religion — and losing part of the treatment in the process. Open on a participant deciding, mid-session, not to mention prayer. Lead on self-censorship as a mechanism rather than a complaint. Call Rabiah Islam at the University of Bath; get a response from an NHS talking-therapies commissioner on training for religious competence.
studies.wider_angle: A broader feature on the secular assumptions embedded in Western psychotherapy — from CBT's cognitive model to conceptions of the self — and the parallel rise of faith-adapted interventions worldwide. Fits a religion-and-society outlet or a general-interest magazine.
studies.caveats: Small qualitative sample (25), not designed to generalize; self-selected participants likely to have had notable experiences; retrospective self-report; single researcher conducting analysis; UK-specific service context.

studies.title: In psilocybin trials, giving the active metabolite may be gentler than the drug itself
studies.ns_score_reason: a genuinely novel within-subject comparison that could reshape trial design, but N=20 healthy volunteers and industry involvement limit it
studies.ns_check: Not verified — SerpAPI unavailable this run
studies.the_study: In a randomized crossover trial, 20 healthy adults (10 men, 10 women, mean age 40) took up to four sessions of botanical whole-mushroom-derived preparations: oral psilocybin (25 mg), oral psilocin (17.5 mg), or sublingual psilocin at three doses. All sessions included therapeutic support and psychotherapy before and after dosing. Oral psilocin produced a subjective and temporal experience much like oral psilocybin, but with fewer adverse effects; sublingual psilocin was well tolerated but delivered apparently lower exposure.
studies.why_it_matters: Nearly every modern psychedelic trial uses synthetic oral psilocybin, which the body must convert to psilocin. Delivering psilocin directly may cut side effects without altering the experience — relevant to how future psychedelic-assisted therapy is actually dosed.
studies.pitch_angle: Skip the prodrug. A crossover trial in which the same 20 people took three different mushroom-derived preparations suggests the active metabolite gives you the same trip with less nausea and cardiovascular load. Open on the logic of why psilocybin was ever the standard. Call Joshua Woolley at UCSF; be explicit about the commercial interest in botanical extracts.
studies.wider_angle: A business-of-psychedelics piece on formulation patents — botanical versus synthetic, sublingual versus oral — as the route to intellectual property in a field built on unpatentable natural molecules. Fits a business or pharmaceutical-industry outlet.
studies.caveats: Small N (20), healthy volunteers rather than patients, no clinical outcomes measured; open-label subjective ratings; sublingual arm not comparable due to lower exposure; formulations supplied by Filament Health Corp., two of whose employees are co-authors; short follow-up.

studies.title: European psychiatrists learn to handle suicide risk mostly by living through a patient's suicide
studies.journal: International Journal of Psychiatry in Clinical Practice
studies.ns_score_reason: an uncomfortable finding about medical training with a clear narrative, weakened by a convenience-sample survey design
studies.ns_check: Not verified — SerpAPI unavailable this run
studies.the_study: A survey of 259 psychiatric trainees and early-career psychiatrists across 36 European countries measured suicide-related knowledge and skills, exposure to patient suicide, and burnout. Average knowledge scores were 76.7 per cent correct, with wide variation between respondents. Those who had experienced at least one patient suicide scored higher on knowledge — and reported less support and supervision afterward. Psychotherapy training and comfort in asking direct questions about suicide both tracked greater perceived competence.
studies.why_it_matters: It suggests that a core clinical skill is being acquired reactively, through adverse events, rather than through structured teaching — and that clinicians who go through the event are left comparatively unsupported.
studies.pitch_angle: The psychiatrists who know most about suicide risk are the ones who have already lost a patient. Open on the aftermath of a patient suicide and the supervision that didn't follow. Note the separate finding that psychotherapy training predicts confidence in asking the direct question. Call Umberto Volpe at the Polytechnic University of Marche, and the European Federation of Psychiatric Trainees.
studies.wider_angle: A medical-education feature on "postvention" — what health systems owe clinicians after a patient death by suicide — alongside the wider literature on second-victim support in medicine. Fits a medical trade publication or a health-focused news outlet.
studies.caveats: Convenience sample of 259 across 36 countries, so country-level comparison is not possible; cross-sectional and self-reported, including the perceived-competence measure; the knowledge–exposure association could run in either direction; respondents self-selected.

studies.title: Indigenous Australians reach mental health services more often but get fewer therapy sessions
studies.journal: Australian & New Zealand Journal of Psychiatry
studies.ns_score_reason: a huge linked administrative dataset with a genuinely unexpected split between access and dose; national policy specificity narrows the appeal
studies.ns_check: Not verified — SerpAPI unavailable this run
studies.the_study: Researchers linked 2021 Census, Medicare Benefits Schedule and Indigenous identifier data for 2,494,381 people in Southeast Queensland, of whom 2.98 per cent were Indigenous. Indigenous residents were *more* likely than non-Indigenous residents to use any subsidized mental health service — but received fewer total sessions, fewer psychotherapy sessions specifically, and waited longer between a mental health care plan and follow-up treatment. Indigenous men, people over 40, and those with unstable housing or lower educational attainment were least likely to use any service at all.
studies.why_it_matters: Access statistics and treatment adequacy are not the same thing. A population can look well served on a headline "any use" figure while receiving substantially less of the treatment that actually requires sustained contact.
studies.pitch_angle: A counterintuitive equity finding: getting through the door more often, getting less therapy once inside. Open on the gap between a care plan and the first follow-up session. Lead on why psychotherapy specifically — the part requiring continuity — is where the shortfall shows. Call Sandra Diminic or Xiaolin Zhou at the Queensland Centre for Mental Health Research, and an Institute for Urban Indigenous Health co-author for the community view.
studies.wider_angle: A health-services feature on how "access" is measured in publicly funded mental health systems worldwide, and why session counts and dropout rates tell a different story from contact rates. Fits a health-policy or public-health outlet.
studies.caveats: Observational administrative data, cannot establish causation; one urban region of Australia, explicitly framed as a case study; Medicare-subsidized services only, so care through Aboriginal community-controlled or state services is not captured; no clinical outcomes.

studies.title: When hypnosis makes facial pain worse, it may be revealing where the pain came from
studies.ns_score_reason: striking clinical idea that reframes treatment failure as diagnostic information, but it is three cases with no controls
studies.ns_check: No recent NS.com coverage found ✓ (0 hits)
studies.the_study: Clinicians at a tertiary orofacial pain clinic describe three patients with chronic facial pain whose symptoms got *worse* during standardized hypnosis sessions. The authors argue these paradoxical reactions were not failures but revealing moments, exposing a link between the physical symptom and emotional distress the patients had not previously articulated. In all three cases, the reaction led patients to engage with psychotherapy they had previously refused.
studies.why_it_matters: Not much yet in terms of hard evidence — but it opens a line of enquiry into whether provoking a symptom can serve as a diagnostic tool in functional and psychogenic pain, and it reframes an adverse response as clinically informative rather than a reason to stop.
studies.pitch_angle: A treatment that makes the symptom worse, and a clinician who treats that as the point. Open on a patient in a dental clinic whose jaw pain spikes under hypnotic induction, and who finally connects it to something they had never said out loud. Frame it around the difficult category of functional symptoms and how patients resist psychological explanations. Call Gil Wasserman and Iftah Biran at Tel Aviv Sourasky Medical Center; get a functional-neurological-disorder specialist for a second opinion.
studies.wider_angle: A feature on the fraught status of functional and psychogenic diagnoses — patients who feel dismissed, clinicians with poor tools, and the hunt for anything that makes the mind-body link tangible to a skeptical patient. Fits a general-interest health magazine or a narrative medicine outlet.
studies.caveats: Case series of three patients, no control group, single center; interpretations are clinical and psychodynamic rather than measured; no outcome data on whether the subsequent psychotherapy helped; risk of harm from deliberately provoking symptoms is not systematically assessed.

trends_raw: _No prior digest on this topic to compare against yet — this is the first run._
feature_pitch_raw:
**The pattern:** Several studies in this batch converge on the same uncomfortable point — psychotherapy research's conclusions are hostage to the instruments and timing it uses. "Whether a patient had a 'sudden gain' in therapy depends on which questionnaire you used" (PMID 40955789) shows a celebrated phenomenon changing not just in frequency but in *which people have it* depending on scale length; "Automated sentiment analysis of therapy sessions barely matches what human coders see" (PMID 42708250) finds near-zero turn-level agreement between machines and humans on emotion, yet both still predict alliance; "Social life doesn't improve during therapy — it improves for years afterward" (PMID 42695247) finds the main relational benefit arriving long after the discharge-day assessment that most trials treat as the endpoint; and "Indigenous Australians reach mental health services more often but get fewer therapy sessions" (PMID 42592892) shows a population looking well served on the headline access metric while receiving substantially less actual treatment. "AI writes usable therapy notes — but misses what clinicians notice" (PMID 42715612) sits in the same space: machine and human accounts of the same session diverge in specific, patterned ways.

**Why pitch this now:** Computational tools are being sold into therapy rooms — AI scribes, sentiment dashboards, session analytics — on the assumption that the underlying measurements are sound, at exactly the moment when studies from within the field are showing that scale choice, measurement timing and proxy metrics can each flip the answer.

**Angle:** A reported piece on the measurement layer beneath psychotherapy evidence, following one question — how do we know therapy worked? — through questionnaires, discharge-day endpoints, session counts and now algorithms, for readers who have been in therapy or are being offered app-based versions of it. Written for a general science audience rather than methodologists, with the automation angle as the news peg.

**Potential headlines:**
- What therapy research measures, and what it misses
- The week everything changed in therapy may depend on which form you filled in
- Your therapy is being scored by instruments that disagree about whether it worked

**Potential outlets:**
- **New Scientist Features** — fits the Mind section's appetite for a rigorous look at how psychological evidence is built, with the AI-in-the-clinic hook giving it immediacy.
- **Undark** — a natural home for a measurement-validity story that implicates both a research literature and a commercial product wave.
- **STAT** — strong for the clinical and vendor side: AI scribes and session analytics entering mental health care ahead of validation.
- **Nature (news feature)** — would take the metascience framing, given the sudden-gains instrument-dependence result sits squarely in the reproducibility conversation.

# Fact-Check Report: New Scientist Story Ideas — Psychotherapy — September 2026
**Checked:** 2026-09-11 | **Studies reviewed:** 14
**Publication:** New Scientist | **Section:** New Scientist Mind

---

# Fact-Check Report — New Scientist Mind story digest (run date 2026-09-11)

---

### Study 1: Exposure therapy for spider phobia works less well when progesterone is high
**PMID:** 42700422 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Headline states an association as a settled effect** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Exposure therapy for spider phobia works less well when progesterone is high"
- **Abstract says:** "higher progesterone levels on the day of exposure therapy were associated with less improvement in behavioral avoidance" and "provide preliminary evidence that ovarian hormones ... *may* affect exposure-based outcomes"
- **Problem:** The headline converts a secondary, correlational, explicitly preliminary finding on one outcome (behavioral avoidance) into a general statement about how well exposure therapy works. The body text and Caveats are appropriately hedged; the headline is not.
- **Suggested fix:** "Higher progesterone on the day of exposure therapy is linked to less improvement in spider-phobia avoidance"

**Issue B. "Everyone improved" overstates a group-level result** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Everyone improved."
- **Abstract says:** "Both phobic fear and avoidance behavior improved significantly over time."
- **Problem:** Significant mean improvement over time is not the same as every participant improving; the abstract reports no individual-level response rates.
- **Suggested fix:** "Fear and avoidance improved significantly across the group over time."

**Issue C. NS fit score of 7 rests on a small, uncontrolled sample with a null primary comparison** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "**NS fit:** 7/10 — genuinely new question ('when does therapy work?') with a clean biological hook, held back by a small sample and a null result on the headline comparison"
- **Abstract says:** "N=45 women"; "improvement did not differ between menstrual cycle groups"; "preliminary evidence"; "More research in larger samples is needed"
- **Problem:** The rationale text already concedes the two problems that should cap the score: N=45, no control group, no randomization to cycle phase, and the only positive result is a secondary hormone–outcome correlation. A 7 implies near-certain commissioning strength.
- **Suggested fix:** Score 6/10, with the same rationale text.

*Note:* Author affiliations ("Susanne Fischer and Ulrike Ehlert at the University of Zurich") are not listed in the abstract record supplied — **unverifiable from abstract only.**

---

### Study 2: People want their psilocybin natural, even when the synthetic version is chemically identical
**PMID:** 42678038 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Significance claim for Study 2 not stated in the abstract** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "in the second study, people were significantly more willing to take psilocybin 'isolated from mushrooms' than an identical synthetic version"
- **Abstract says:** "In Study 2, we found that participants had stronger intentions to use a natural version of psilocybin isolated from mushrooms as compared to an identical synthetic version..."
- **Problem:** The abstract flags significance explicitly for Study 1 ("significantly lower intentions") but not for the Study 2 comparison. The digest adds "significantly" where the abstract does not.
- **Suggested fix:** "people reported stronger intentions to take psilocybin 'isolated from mushrooms' than an identical synthetic version"

**Issue B. Caveats contain details not in the abstract** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "online convenience samples of unclear representativeness"; "population may not generalize beyond the US"
- **Abstract says:** "two studies involving independent samples (total N = 1,102)" — no recruitment mode, sampling frame or country stated.
- **Problem:** The mode of administration and national composition of the samples are **unverifiable from abstract only**. The inference is plausible (all authors are US-based) but should not be stated as fact.
- **Suggested fix:** "Sampling frame and recruitment method not specified in the abstract; likely US-based samples, so generalisability is unclear"

**Issue C. NS fit of 7 rests on hypothetical, self-reported intentions** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "**NS fit:** 7/10 ... limited by the fact that intentions are not behavior"
- **Abstract says:** "we examined the intentions to use psilocybin in a mental health context"
- **Problem:** All outcomes are hypothetical willingness ratings plus self-reported depression, mindfulness and narcissism scales. The large N supports precision, not validity. A 7 overstates the strength of the evidence base for the claim being made about real-world uptake.
- **Suggested fix:** Score 6/10.

### Study 3: Psychotherapy use in the US jumped 41 per cent in four years — and worsening mental health explains only a third of it
**PMID:** 42723007 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Headline attaches the decomposition figure to the wrong outcome** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "Psychotherapy use in the US jumped 41 per cent in four years — and worsening mental health explains only a third of it"
- **Abstract says:** "Decomposition analysis suggested that 36.7% of the increase in **mental health care use** was associated with changes in depression and anxiety"
- **Problem:** The 36.7% figure decomposes the rise in *any* mental health care use (19.2% → 23.8%), not the psychotherapy-specific rise. The digest body gets this right ("36.7 per cent of the overall rise"), but the headline welds the 41% psychotherapy figure to the 36.7% overall-care decomposition, implying a decomposition of psychotherapy use that the abstract does not report.
- **Suggested fix:** "US psychotherapy use jumped 41 per cent in four years — and symptoms explain only a third of the wider rise in mental health care"

**Issue B. Decomposition language edges toward causal attribution** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Decomposition analysis attributed 36.7 per cent of the overall rise to changes in anxiety and depression symptoms and 11.3 per cent to insurance coverage"
- **Abstract says:** "36.7% of the increase in mental health care use was **associated with** changes in depression and anxiety, whereas 11.3% was associated with changes in health insurance coverage"
- **Problem:** "Attributed to" reads as causal apportionment; the abstract keeps the language associational throughout. The Caveats correctly note causation cannot be established, so the body text should match.
- **Suggested fix:** "Decomposition analysis associated 36.7 per cent of the overall rise with changes in anxiety and depression symptoms and 11.3 per cent with insurance coverage"

### Study 4: Children's therapy works better when the therapist unconsciously mirrors them
**PMID:** 42721331 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. "Active ingredient ... rather than anything said out loud" is not supported** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "suggests the active ingredient in play therapy may be bodily synchrony rather than anything said out loud"
- **Abstract says:** "therapists' nonverbal coordination supports therapeutic change in Mentalization-Based Treatment for Children by enhancing children's affect regulatory capacities within play"
- **Problem:** The study coded nonverbal coordination and in-session affect regulation; it did not measure or model verbal interventions, so it cannot rank bodily synchrony against speech. The digest sets up a comparison the study never ran.
- **Suggested fix:** "suggests that therapists' bodily coordination with a child is an active contributor to change in play therapy, alongside what is said"

**Issue B. "Unconsciously" is an addition** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Children's therapy works better when the therapist unconsciously mirrors them"
- **Abstract says:** "therapists' nonverbal coordination"
- **Problem:** Nothing in the abstract addresses whether the coordination was conscious, deliberate or automatic. The word is doing rhetorical work the data don't support.
- **Suggested fix:** "Children's therapy works better when the therapist's movements sync with theirs"

**Issue C. "Entirely" overstates the mediation result** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "The effect of nonverbal coordination on outcomes ran entirely through in-session regulation; the direct path was not significant."
- **Abstract says:** "Indirect effects ... were significant, whereas direct effects were not, indicating that nonverbal coordination was associated with outcomes **primarily** through in-session affect regulation"
- **Problem:** A non-significant direct path is not a zero direct path; the authors say "primarily", not "entirely".
- **Suggested fix:** "The effect of nonverbal coordination on outcomes ran primarily through in-session regulation; the direct path was not significant."

**Issue D. Behavioural specifics not in the abstract** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "more nonverbal coordination — matching posture, rhythm and movement during play"
- **Abstract says:** "coded for therapists' nonverbal coordination"
- **Problem:** The specific coded channels (posture, rhythm, movement) are **unverifiable from abstract only**.
- **Suggested fix:** "more nonverbal coordination with the child during play (as rated by trained coders)"

### Study 5: Social life doesn't improve during therapy — it improves for years afterward
**PMID:** 42695247 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Pitch attributes post-treatment growth to therapy, contradicting the digest's own caveat** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "**Pitch angle:** Therapy's social payoff arrives late — sometimes years after the last session."
- **Abstract says:** "There was significant growth in QQSR across long-term follow-up ... There was no change from pre- to posttreatment"; design is naturalistic with no control group
- **Problem:** The study observed growth *after* treatment in an uncontrolled sample; it cannot show that therapy produced it (maturation, regression to the mean and life events are unmodelled alternatives). The Caveats say "cannot establish causation", but the pitch line asserts a therapy "payoff". Body and caveat contradict each other.
- **Suggested fix:** "Social connection keeps improving in the years after therapy ends — even though it didn't shift during treatment"

**Issue B. Self-affiliation glossed as self-compassion** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "It also offers evidence for the long-suspected loop between self-compassion and friendship running in both directions."
- **Abstract says:** "the Structural Analysis of Social Behavior Introject **self-affiliation**"; "A friendly relationship to oneself"
- **Problem:** SASB introject self-affiliation is a specific construct, not the self-compassion scale readers will assume. Also worth noting the authors' own caution, omitted from the digest: "The QQSR might measure relatively stable characteristics."
- **Suggested fix:** "It also offers evidence for a two-way loop between social connection and a warm relationship to oneself (measured as SASB self-affiliation)."

### Study 6: AI writes usable therapy notes — but misses what clinicians notice
**PMID:** 42715612 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Rater identity claim not in the abstract** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "evaluation by expert raters, not by the clinicians or clients involved"
- **Abstract says:** "Blinded-to-source judges evaluated the summaries on factual consistency, salient meaning preservation, and clinical value."
- **Problem:** The abstract does not state the judges' expertise or their relationship to the sessions. **Unverifiable from abstract only.**
- **Suggested fix:** "evaluation by blinded judges whose expertise and independence from the sessions are not specified in the abstract"

Everything else — 1,008 summaries (504/504), 108 five-minute segments, 36 sessions, clinicians rated higher overall, LLM superior on central themes, no difference on clinical value for therapeutic relationship and intrapersonal functioning, "first direct comparison", draft-and-review conclusion — matches the abstract.

### Study 7: Automated sentiment analysis of therapy sessions barely matches what human coders see
**PMID:** 42708250 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. "Predicted" overstates a dyadic association** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Both tools nonetheless predicted therapist- and client-rated early alliance."
- **Abstract says:** "Automated sentiment was dyadically associated with therapist- and client-reported early alliance."
- **Problem:** Two changes: "associated with" becomes "predicted" (directional/causal lean), and the abstract does not break the alliance result out by tool, so "both tools" is not established.
- **Suggested fix:** "Automated sentiment was nonetheless associated with therapist- and client-rated early alliance."

The turn-level null convergence, the weak session-level convergence, the client-versus-therapist negativity finding, the 108 sessions, LIWC and XLM-T, and Peluso's Florida State affiliation all check out.

### Study 8: Whether a patient had a "sudden gain" in therapy depends on which questionnaire you used
**PMID:** 40955789 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. "Overturns prior research" overstates the novelty category** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "**Novelty:** Overturns prior research"
- **Abstract says:** "These results seem to raise important questions about the detection of sudden gains, and the comparability of findings across studies using different measures."
- **Problem:** The paper raises a measurement-comparability caution; it does not test or refute prior substantive findings about sudden gains. The authors' own framing is "a reason for caution".
- **Suggested fix:** "**Novelty:** Methodological challenge to an established literature"

**Issue B. "Artifact of the questionnaire" goes beyond the finding** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "the week everything suddenly shifts — may be partly an artifact of the questionnaire"
- **Abstract says:** "the standard and ultra-brief measures identified different individuals as having experienced a sudden gain"
- **Problem:** Measure-dependent *identification* is a detection problem; it does not establish that the phenomenon itself is an artifact. Also worth noting the abstract's directional detail the digest smooths over: more sudden gains by PHQ-9 than PHQ-2, but more by GAD-2 than GAD-7.
- **Suggested fix:** "the week everything suddenly shifts — may be harder to pin down than the literature assumes, because who counts as having had one depends on the scale"

### Study 9: Trauma-focused therapy for PTSD plus addiction helps veterans more than civilians
**PMID:** 41114957 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Safety claim the study did not test** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "it addresses the persistent clinical worry that trauma-focused therapy destabilizes people who are drinking. It did not; it helped."
- **Abstract says:** "trauma-focused psychotherapy targeting PTSD and integrated trauma-focused psychotherapy ... were both superior to treatment as usual for alcohol use severity outcomes"
- **Problem:** Superiority on a group-mean alcohol severity outcome is not a test of destabilisation, dropout or adverse events, none of which the abstract reports. "It did not" asserts a safety finding not in evidence, and a reader could take it as clearance to proceed clinically.
- **Suggested fix:** "it speaks to the persistent clinical worry about trauma-focused therapy in people who are drinking: on alcohol severity outcomes, these therapies outperformed treatment as usual. The abstract reports no data on adverse events or dropout."

**Issue B. Headline generalises a single-domain effect** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Trauma-focused therapy for PTSD plus addiction helps veterans more than civilians"
- **Abstract says:** "this effect was stronger for veterans than civilians" (alcohol use severity only); "Analyses did not provide evidence for differential response ... on PTSD or drug use severity outcomes as a function of veteran status."
- **Problem:** The veteran advantage exists on one of three outcome domains. The body text and Caveats say so; the headline does not.
- **Suggested fix:** "Trauma-focused therapy for PTSD plus addiction cuts drinking more in veterans than civilians"

Funding (NIAAA) and the COPE-manual/industry conflicts are both disclosed in the Caveats — correctly handled.

### Study 10: Muslim clients say they censor their faith in the therapy room
**PMID:** 42068016 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. "Visible discomfort" is not what the abstract reports** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "barriers — therapists' visible discomfort and limited knowledge, secular service frameworks, and clients' resulting self-censorship"
- **Abstract says:** "perceived barriers to discussing religion in therapy reflected therapists' **limited confidence and knowledge**, secular service frameworks and participants' resulting self-censorship"
- **Problem:** "Limited confidence" becomes "visible discomfort", a stronger and more behavioural claim. The pitch angle then compounds it ("Clients are managing their therapists' discomfort about religion").
- **Suggested fix:** "barriers — therapists' limited confidence and knowledge, secular service frameworks, and clients' resulting self-censorship"; and in the pitch, "Clients are working around their therapists' uncertainty about religion".

Sample (25 UK Muslim adults, NHS and private), reflexive thematic analysis, the two overarching themes, and the Bath affiliation all check out.

### Study 11: In psilocybin trials, giving the active metabolite may be gentler than the drug itself
**PMID:** 42668404 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Specific side effects named that the abstract does not name** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "suggests the active metabolite gives you the same trip with less nausea and cardiovascular load"
- **Abstract says:** "Oral psilocin produced a similar temporal and subjective profile to oral psilocybin, with a **lower burden of adverse effects**."
- **Problem:** The abstract reports adverse effect burden in aggregate and mentions vital signs as an assessment method, but does not specify nausea or cardiovascular outcomes. **Unverifiable from abstract only.**
- **Suggested fix:** "suggests the active metabolite gives a comparable experience with a lower overall burden of adverse effects"

Design (randomized within-subject crossover, N=20, 10 men/10 women, mean age 40.1), doses, therapeutic support, and the sublingual exposure caveat are all accurate, and the Filament Health Corp. involvement is disclosed in the Caveats.

### Study 12: European psychiatrists learn to handle suicide risk mostly by living through a patient's suicide
**PMID:** 42622500 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. "Mostly" / "rather than" overstate the authors' own hedge** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "European psychiatrists learn to handle suicide risk mostly by living through a patient's suicide" and "a core clinical skill is being acquired reactively, through adverse events, rather than through structured teaching"
- **Abstract says:** "Exposure to patient suicide is associated with higher knowledge levels, suggesting that learning may rely **partly** on experiential rather than structured training pathways."
- **Problem:** The finding is a cross-sectional association between exposure and higher knowledge scores, which the authors interpret as a *partial* reliance on experiential learning. The digest upgrades "partly" to "mostly" and to an exclusive "rather than". The Caveats correctly note the association could run in either direction, but the headline and Why-it-matters do not reflect that.
- **Suggested fix:** Headline: "European psychiatrists who have lost a patient to suicide score higher on suicide knowledge — and get less support afterwards." Why it matters: "It suggests a core clinical skill may be acquired partly through adverse events rather than structured teaching — and that clinicians who go through the event are left comparatively unsupported."

Mean SKSQ score (76.7%), N=259 across 36 countries, the psychotherapy-training and comfort associations, and the Volpe affiliation all check out.

### Study 13: Indigenous Australians reach mental health services more often but get fewer therapy sessions
**PMID:** 42592892 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Headline generalises a single urban region to a national population** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Indigenous Australians reach mental health services more often but get fewer therapy sessions"
- **Abstract says:** "an urban Indigenous population"; "2,494,381 individuals (2.98% Indigenous) in Southeast Queensland residents"; title: "A case study from Southeast Queensland"
- **Problem:** The authors explicitly frame this as a single-region urban case study. The Caveats flag it, but the headline reads as a national finding.
- **Suggested fix:** "In urban Southeast Queensland, Indigenous residents reach mental health services more often but get fewer therapy sessions"

Minor wording note: the abstract says these subgroups were "less likely to use any services"; the digest says "least likely", a small strengthening. Everything else — linked 2021 Census/MBS data, higher any-use, fewer total and psychotherapy sessions, longer waits between care plan and follow-up, subgroup predictors, and the QCMHR affiliations — is accurate.

### Study 14: When hypnosis makes facial pain worse, it may be revealing where the pain came from
**PMID:** 42685357 | **Verdict:** ✅ Accurate

No factual errors found. Framing is consistent with the abstract: three patients, tertiary orofacial pain clinic, standardized hypnotic sessions, symptom exacerbation interpreted as diagnostically meaningful rather than a treatment failure, and subsequent engagement with previously resisted psychotherapy. The hedging ("may be revealing", "Not much yet in terms of hard evidence") is appropriate for a three-case series, the Caveats are complete, and the NS fit of 4/10 is well calibrated to the evidence.
